findings.text: Queries are sometimes raised on documents that only fall due at a later stage (e.g., an FSSAI licence queried at CTE stage, although it is required only at the operation stage).
Queries are raised repeatedly, one at a time, rather than being consolidated; one participant had to approach the Industries Department to have the practice looked into.
No user manual or video guidance exists on the portal, which participants said is the reason they must take help from consultants.
The application provides only one or two places to upload additional documents, making it hard for the scrutinising officer to tell where a particular document has been placed.
A one-year validity option appears in the fee table but does not appear when applying online; participants could not say whether this was a technical error.
Payment slips are occasionally not generated even though the amount is debited, requiring a visit to the department's computer section to retrieve the slip.
The portal is at times not working, and uploads are limited by file size/format (PDF/JPG) with no in-portal resizing tool.
No ticketing system exists on the portal for grievances; problems can only be raised by phone or email without tracking.

The fee is payable only in whole years with no month-wise proration; a unit needing 1.5 years must pay for two full years, and unused prepaid years at CTE are neither refunded nor adjusted when CTO is obtained earlier.
If a unit is not set up within the first year, CTE is renewed for a further year at the same fee as a fresh application.

The ~25-page application form contains technical terminology (particularly the stack-emission section) that even technically qualified applicants cannot follow; one participant abandoned the process on first attempt and reapplied years later through an agency, at a consultant cost of roughly ₹1-1.5 lakh.
Session-2 participants openly alleged that money is demanded during the process, with approval reportedly immediate if paid (amount cited around ₹1.5 lakh) and delayed to three-four months otherwise.
Session-2 participants said no officer communicated any timeline and none is displayed on the portal; approvals in practice took 45 days to 3 months.

Despite being described as online, applicants still must visit the office as the file moves table to table; one participant called it an 'eyewash'. The portal also locks to one district, so an applicant cannot view another district's application status without closing the session.

Pollution category is assigned without recorded reasons or a published checklist; one R&D unit was placed in red category with no explanation and only converted to orange after personal representation, while a similar unit elsewhere was green.

DIC and the Pollution Control Board each require the other's clearance first, creating a circular requirement that can take an applicant 3-4 years merely to set up a unit; a 2021 order exempting unsubsidised units on private land from DIC registration has reportedly not been implemented or communicated to departments.

Validity is one year on first grant and a minimum of two years on renewal, counted from date of issue (not application), with no shorter option even where only 3-6 months are needed; one case was relaxed only after departmental intervention.

Documents (including DIC registration) are resubmitted in full at renewal, and the same CTE documents plus a lab test report are demanded again for Consent to Operate even though the department already holds them.

Session-1 participants said the process is generally working well, that the single window retains and auto-retrieves previously uploaded documents for other services, and that refunds of failed payments have not been a problem.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: If the fee is twenty thousand rupees for a year and I need one and a half years, I have to pay forty thousand rupees.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: Deemed approval is there, but in my years of service I recall it being given in only one or two cases.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: If you give, you get it immediately. If you do not give, it takes three months, four months.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The application form is so complicated that I gave up the first time and applied years later through an agency.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: A similar research and development company was given green category and I was given red, with no reason and no checklist.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: It is only an eyewash. You apply online and then you still go from table to table.

gaps.text: ED states the statutory CTE decision ceiling is 120 days. FGD session 1 participants instead cite a 90-day maximum ('the maximum period is ninety days'), a different stated statutory ceiling from the one the official gave.

ED describes the CTE fee as a one-time fee based on capital investment/project cost and category. FGD participants describe it as effectively an annual fee payable only in whole years with no proration, and say unused prepaid years are forfeited rather than refunded or adjusted — a different fee structure from the one-time characterisation in the ED.

The ED officer stated there is no major structural bottleneck from the department's side, with most friction attributed to applicant-side issues (form-filling, delayed query responses). FGD session 2 participants instead described alleged solicitation of money for faster approval, opaque category assignment with no checklist, and a circular DIC/PCC clearance deadlock lasting years — a materially different account of where the friction lies.
FGD corroborates the ED's statements that PAN/Aadhaar are not required at CTE stage and that a deemed-approval provision exists but is rarely invoked in practice.

No single average processing time emerges from the FGD: session 1 (generally positive) cites 10-15 days typical; session 2 (critical) cites 45 days to 3 months, and attendees in session 2 said no timeline was ever communicated to them at all.

findings.text: The fee for the full validity period (now 5 years, sometimes 10) is collected entirely upfront with no shorter option, even where a unit expects to convert from CTE within a year; one orange-category participant cited a fee of about ₹3 lakh for 5 years.
The fee is generated automatically by a portal calculator only after the form is submitted, and there is no one the applicant can ask to question or explain the amount.
The fee is perceived as high and is said to rise every year, with participants unsure whether the increase is government-mandated or why it applies.

Mobile number/email entered at first registration are frozen (sometimes a consultant's/CA's details), requiring an office visit to change; after a data migration some contact fields were blank, blocking new service applications for several months.
Uploaded documents cannot be viewed, opened, or replaced; filenames must be unique with no spaces; there is no draft-save option.
Query notifications by email/message are unreliable; applicants often learn of a query only by chance or by calling the department.
The portal lost already-uploaded documents on one occasion (attributed by the department to a cyber attack), requiring re-upload and causing subsequent payment issues.
No training or user manual is provided for CTO or any other single-window service; applicants learn the process by themselves.

The tracking page shows only file movement between field and division officers; exceeding a stated internal period (e.g., 15 to 20 days) carries no consequence for the department, and 90 days was called too long.
Validity is now fixed at 5 years with inconsistent communication (some told 5 years, some 2); participants asked that the earlier choice of one, two, three or five years be restored.
Participants state no deemed-approval provision exists for CTO; where the officer takes no action within the prescribed period the application is auto-rejected rather than approved.

The GST registration number is insisted upon even where a unit is exempt below the ₹20 lakh turnover threshold; an exemption certificate may be offered but can still draw an objection, so applicants obtain GST registration at the outset regardless.
The detailed project report and other CTE-stage documents (registration, land allotment, CTE itself) must be re-uploaded for CTO even though already on departmental record.

Site inspection covers effluent/sewage treatment plants, machinery, pollution-control equipment, cleanliness, plantation, ventilation, and geo-tagged photographs, with other departments' clearances verified; approval routes from field officer to district officer and, for higher categories, to the Chairman.

Session-2 (hotel sector) participants said room-count-based categorisation does not reflect actual pollution load; generator sets and kitchens attract further clearances irrespective of actual discharge.
Hotels have been granted industry status but not industry benefits such as power subsidy, despite representations on the point.

An auto-renewal facility secured for small green-category hotels (fewer than 20 rooms, no site visit) was subsequently narrowed by a rider that brought the matter back under departmental control, which participants believed was done to preserve the visit and its associated payment.

Although told no office visit is required, applicants must go in person to learn application status since nothing is pushed to them; a department changing its own coding without notice breaks single-window integration, leaving some of the 261 listed services non-functional online.

Participants described the department as cooperative and the process as predictable, though noted that in other states the district industries office is more proactive in guiding units, whereas in J&K the applicant must take the initiative.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Earlier we had the option of one year, two years or five years. Now they say take five years.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Ninety days is too long. If the officer does not act in forty five days, it should be deemed approved.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The mobile number and email we entered first cannot be changed. For that we have to go to the department.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: If a department changes its coding without informing anyone, the integration on the single window breaks.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The fee comes from the calculator on the portal itself. We cannot ask anyone about it.

gaps.text: ED states a deemed-approval provision technically exists for CTO after the 120-day statutory period (though rarely invoked). FGD participants in both sessions state no deemed-approval provision exists for CTO at all, and that non-action by the officer instead leads to auto-rejection rather than any approval safeguard.

ED's stated timeline basis for CTO is a 120-day statutory maximum. FGD session 1 participants describe the prescribed period as ninety days ('ninety days is too long...') and ask it be cut to forty-five — a different ceiling from the ED's 120 days.

ED gives CTO validity as category-based: Green 15 years, Orange 10 years, Red 5 years. FGD (both sessions) describes current practice as a flat minimum of five years (sometimes extended to ten), with the earlier 1/2/3-year options discontinued — not matching the 15/10/5-year tiered structure the official described.
No participant's cited fee figure (~₹3 lakh for 5 years, orange category) was cross-checked against a complete capital-investment/category fee schedule; only one worked example was captured.
FGD corroborates the ED's point that no unnecessary document beyond the standard set was demanded and that no physical office visit is needed after applying — process is otherwise online end-to-end.

findings.text: The portal rejects files above about 300 KB, forcing applicants to compress scanned plans/papers using an external tool before re-uploading.
The portal occasionally hangs or does not open, though participants said it mostly works easily.

Applicants depend on a chartered accountant/consultant to file; officials interact with the consultant rather than management during site visits, and no departmental help desk was known to participants.
Participants did not know any prescribed processing timeline and were unaware of any deemed-approval provision; the actual time depends on when the inspector visits.
No grievance mechanism was known to participants; applicants said they generally choose not to complain and attend to their own business instead.
Udyam registration is not required for the factory licence itself but must be held separately to access any central government scheme.
Newly introduced requirements (a 'date of production' requirement and a fire-clearance requirement) were not understood or explained to participants.

The same pollution certificate is required separately for the factory licence and again for the electricity connection; participants said the portal functions more like a 'multi window' than a single window since each department asks again.
The site plan has to be uploaded as many as twenty times at different places within the application, which participants said fills government server storage unnecessarily.
Officers physically check the building plan and sale deed on a site visit; at renewal, a comprehensive team including fire and pollution officers inspects together.
Processing time depends mainly on when the factory inspector visits, though the department's overall response time was considered good.
Raise the file-size cap to about 1,000 KB or add an automatic in-portal compression tool.
Integrate the portal with a central server so a document uploaded once is verified by all departments automatically, on the model used by the transport office for vehicles.

Participants said the process has improved considerably since it was manual, and is faster now that Jammu and Kashmir is a Union Territory; a chartered accountant retained for all compliance work costs about ₹50,000/year with no other hidden cost reported.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The same pollution certificate is asked for the factory licence and again for the electricity connection.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: This is not a single window. It is a multi window, because each department asks again.
quotes.topic: Single window not functioning as intended

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The site plan is uploaded again and again, up to twenty times, and the government pays for the server.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: If a document is uploaded once, the other departments should check it on the central server, as the transport office does.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: We do not know within how many days the licence should come. It depends on when the inspector visits.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: My chartered accountant does all the work and attends the visit. I have no contact with the officers.

gaps.text: ED describes a defined 30-day statutory processing timeline under the Public Services Guarantee Act, 2018 for factory licence applications. FGD participants in this session said they were not aware of any prescribed timeline at all and that actual time depends entirely on when the inspector visits — a mismatch between the formally stated regime and applicants' lived awareness of it.

The ED's document list (pollution NOC, authorised-manager letter, power sanction, fire NOC, site/building plan, lease deed, constitution docs, Aadhaar/bank details, Form 23) and the FGD's list (approved building plan, sale deed/rent agreement, pollution certificate, GST certificate, fire clearance, Aadhaar) only partly overlap; it is unclear whether this reflects genuinely different document sets at different points of the process or incomplete participant recall.

FGD corroborates the ED's finding that no deemed-approval mechanism currently exists for the factory licence, and separately confirms the ED's note of a 'transformation phase' — participants describe the process as considerably improved since J&K became a Union Territory.
No participant gave a cost/fee figure for the factory licence; the ED gap noting the fee structure was never captured remains unresolved by the FGD.

findings.text: The portal logs users out after being left idle for as little as two or three minutes, losing unsaved work, with no option to save the application as a draft.
Uploaded documents cannot be viewed, deleted or modified on the portal; documents from earlier years remain listed alongside the current year's, causing confusion.
Employer-profile fields (name, photo, email, phone) cannot be edited by the user; if the person who set up the account leaves the company, access cannot be transferred to a successor.
The late fee charged for delay is not shown anywhere on the portal or the printed receipt, which shows only the annual fee, even though the full (higher) amount is debited.
The 60-day pre-expiry filing window is not displayed on the portal; participants know it only from having renewed in previous years.
No training or guidance is available for new users; applicants rely on informally telephoning departmental officers for help.
Validity is fixed at 5 years (red) / 10 years (green) with no shorter 1-2 year option available online.
GST registration is mandatory for the renewal application even for a small unit; a self-declaration in its place is not accepted, though the Udyam number is not mandatory.
One-time documents (company PAN, owner PAN, GST certificate) must be re-uploaded at every renewal despite being unchanged.
The fee is paid online only (net banking, debit or credit card); there is no NEFT or bank-challan option.

Portal downtime once delayed an application; the department advised offline submission, issued a provisional certificate, and granted renewal from the same date, with the offline documents re-uploaded once the system was restored.
No intimation is sent when a non-conformity/query is raised; applicants must telephone the department to find out, sometimes only learning two to three days later.
Session-2 (timber/pharma/food) participants reported the portal is frequently down; one applicant tried submitting the same application six times, with entered data lost on each failed submission.
No intimation is sent before a consent expires; the first communication received is often a notice issued only after the consent has already lapsed.
Requirements are conveyed orally with nothing given in writing and no checklist against which an objection can be tested, leading to disputes over what is required.

A paper-trade unit whose waste is sold to a dealer for reprocessing (generating no pollution, in the participant's account) was nonetheless categorised Orange and required to produce a disposal certificate.
Session-2 participants stated that money passes 'under the table' at the inspection stage.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: The portal logs us out if we leave it for even two or three minutes while we are working.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: The PAN card and the GST certificate are one time documents. They should stay on record and not be uploaded again and again.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: The full amount is debited, but the receipt shows only the annual fee. The late fee is not shown anywhere.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The portal is down very often. We tried to submit the same application six times.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: No intimation, no notice, nothing comes before the consent expires.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: My paper goes to the waste dealer and then to the mill. Where is the pollution? Yet I am in orange category.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Under the table money is given at the inspection stage.

gaps.text: ED states DPR is generally not required again at renewal unless there is a change. FGD (session 2) participants state the project report is required again at every renewal even where project details are unchanged ('every document filed at the first application is demanded again... including the project report, which is required again at renewal even though the project details remain unchanged').

ED gives category-based renewal validity of Green 15 / Orange 10 / Red 5 years (same as fresh CTO). FGD session 1 cites five years for red category and ten years for green category — a lower green-category figure than the ED's 15 years, with no participant citing 15 years for any category.

The two FGD sessions give conflicting internal accounts of validity flexibility: session 1 insists the 5/10-year validity 'cannot be reduced' with no 1-2 year option, while session 2 describes white-category units obtaining lifetime validity and green-category units being eligible for auto-renewal — not reconciled between the two sessions.

FGD broadly corroborates the ED's point that renewal fees are lower than fresh fees (fee described as calculated on capital/area/category/size), though no participant cited the ED's specific ₹14,000→₹9,800 example.
No participant quantified the renewal fee schedule precisely enough to independently verify the ED's single worked example.

findings.text: The renewal fee was raised roughly threefold (from ₹5,680 to ₹16,000) with no rationale given despite enquiries; applicants who filed before the notification paid the lower amount, those after paid the higher.

Payments are sometimes deducted but not credited to the department, with no receipt generated; one participant's payment was deducted twice with no refund, which participants described as their principal recurring concern across services.
Applications remain shown as 'pending' on the portal even after an offline provisional certificate has been issued; resubmission requires a further office visit and fee.
Queries are raised at the end of the department's 45-day window, shifting the appearance of delay onto the applicant; one participant had queries raised about five times.
Officers handling a matter are sometimes transferred mid-process, leaving applications unattended with no successor assigned; participants reported holding only provisional certificates as a result.
No prescribed or displayed renewal timeline exists; actual approval has taken between 15 and 60 days in practice.
The several licences a factory must hold (factory licence, solvent storage licence, fire clearance, weights & measures) each run on a different period, forcing near-continuous renewal activity.
Third-shift permission must be renewed every six months even though the underlying factory licence may run for five years.
The fee already paid is forfeited (not carried forward) when capacity is enhanced within the validity period, requiring the full fee to be paid again.

Clearances from other departments (Consent to Operate, fire clearance, power sanction) are re-demanded at every renewal though already on record elsewhere; certificates valid for 3-5 years must still be produced annually, and labour registers/salary particulars (Forms 2 & 3) are refiled yearly despite the department holding prior returns.
Portal downtime and unannounced departmental coding changes break single-window integration, forcing offline filing and repeat fee payment.
Explain and review the threefold fee increase, and extend the validity period proportionately if fees are raised.
Fix and display a definite renewal timeline, with the licence treated as renewed (deemed approval) where the department does not decide within it.

Queries for this service are communicated by phone and message, which participants said works, unlike other services with no communication; a newly placed ease-of-doing-business team in Jammu was said to be taking up the confiscated-fee issue.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The fee was five thousand six hundred and eighty rupees. It has been made sixteen thousand.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The fee gets confiscated. It is deducted from us but the department does not receive it.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: They have forty five days, so they raise the query in the last minute and the delay is shown against us.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: We all have only provisional certificates. The officers were transferred and nobody is there now.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: There is no service at all in which there is deemed approval.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: If a certificate has been given for three years, why should it be produced again every year?

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The factory licence is for five years but the permission for the third shift comes for six months at a time.

gaps.text: ED states no separate renewal-specific timeline exists, referencing the general 30-day factory-licence benchmark. FGD participants instead describe a distinct, department-cited 45-day period governing renewal decisions ('they have forty five days, so they raise the query in the last minute') — a different figure from the ED's 30-day reference point.

The ED flagged that no numerical renewal fee was captured; FGD participants supplied one concrete figure (a threefold rise from ₹5,680 to ₹16,000) but without a full fee schedule or stated rationale, so the complete fee structure remains uncaptured.
FGD corroborates the ED's finding that no deemed-approval mechanism exists for factory-licence renewal in J&K ('There is no service at all in which there is deemed approval').

The ED's own gap on whether physical inspection is mandatory at every renewal (an inconsistency within the ED itself) is not resolved by the FGD, which does not directly address inspection frequency/mandate at renewal.

findings.text: NOCs are required from a large number of departments (including electricity and water supply), each pursued individually by the applicant.

Fees are charged in layers — a non-refundable ₹700 application fee, a building fee (₹80/sqm residential, ₹270/sqm commercial), a scrutiny fee (₹18/sqm both), and a change-of-land-use fee (one case cited at roughly ₹33-34 lakh); the scrutiny fee was seen as an extra burden ultimately passed to the public.

A third-party Auto DCR software scrutinises drawings, overriding the department's own software, in a complicated format; previously accepted PDF drawings no longer suffice, raising cost/time for professionals passed on to clients.
The Auto DCR software sometimes raises invalid discrepancies because it misreads a drawing, and a drawing awaiting approval can be auto-reverted if the software is updated mid-review.
Files are reverted with objections even after the scrutiny fee has been paid, with no fixed time limit for rectification and resubmission.
Portal terminology differs from field usage; a user manual exists but is hard to find, and rural applicants with low computer literacy are especially vulnerable to exploitation.
The system is operated end-to-end by a private company, is not open-source, and every problem's resolution depends on that company, sometimes taking up to two days.
A departmental representative acknowledged revenue-department records are not fully updated online, so an auto-generated plot number may not match actual ground records.
The applicant bears significant coordination effort; one automobile-dealership team of four colleagues spent roughly 15 person-days managing the application alongside their regular duties.

Participants argued the large number of NOCs is not justified for routine cases now that data is online and plot size is verifiable on Google Maps; only title verification plus safety NOCs (e.g., fire) were seen as genuinely necessary.
Permission is taken in multiple sequential stages (stage one, stage two, completion certificate, occupancy certificate, and a further NOC after occupancy) without consolidation.
The change-of-land-use certificate already verifies title, yet the subsequent revenue NOC for building permission repeats the same verification.

All NOCs must be re-obtained if a resubmitted file includes any change, since previously obtained NOCs lapse; the completion/occupancy stage repeats about 70-80% of the same documents and steps, including re-uploading all permissions for a further post-occupancy NOC.

Collecting NOCs from different departments took about one and a half months of a roughly three-month total process in one participant's case; time to prepare/clear a file under the Auto DCR regime has risen 'almost ten times' versus the earlier process.
Reduce NOCs to title verification alone for routine residential/commercial cases, retaining safety NOCs like fire only where required.
Set up in-house facilitation centres in every municipality for rural applicants, with a more prominent user manual and a working customer-care channel.

Participants welcomed a recent reform fixing department-wise NOC-issuance timelines, and said online submission, status tracking and document carry-forward within the portal generally work well; the department reported no complaint about applying online.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The auto DCR needs to be simplified. Professionals are facing a lot of complexity in it.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The time to prepare a file has gone up almost ten times.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: It took us about one and a half months just to gather the NOCs from different departments.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Title verification is the only NOC that is needed. Everything is online today, even the plot size is cross checked on Google Maps.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: For change of land use we submit the revenue documents, and then again for the revenue NOC. That is repetition of the job.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Why are so many stages of permission required, stage one, stage two, completion and then occupancy?

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Rural applicants do not have this level of awareness. Facilitation centres should be the top priority.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The whole system has been taken over by a private company, so for every problem we have to depend on them.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Housing & Urban Development Department / municipal bodies (within municipal committee, council and corporation limits; district authorities handle areas beyond those limits offline), via the Housing Department's own online building-permission portal integrated with the JK Single Window / National Single Window System. The transcript does not precisely name the statutory issuing authority (e.g., Building Operation Controlling Authority vs municipal corporation).

portal.name: Housing Department's online building-permission portal, on the JK Single Window / National Single Window System (within municipal limits; offline at the district level beyond those limits)

timeline.basis: A period of 30 days has reportedly been fixed for approval and 21 days for NOCs, but one participant's actual case took about 3 months overall, roughly 1.5 months of which was spent collecting NOCs from different departments.
timeline.text: Stated internal periods (30 days for approval, 21 days for NOCs) do not match the real-world experience cited, which ran to about three months in one case due to NOC collection and Auto DCR scrutiny delays.

documents: Change-of-land-use certificate (mandatory for commercial buildings and residential plots above 1 kanal)
NOCs from multiple departments (e.g., electricity, water supply, fire, health)
licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED. The precise full list and count of NOCs required (beyond electricity, water supply, fire and health, named individually) was not captured.

deemedApproval.text: A deemed-approval provision was said to exist 'subject to conditions' (examination of bylaws and ownership), but participants indicated that in practice an applicant must simply wait for the officer to act, leaving its real-world operability unclear.

validity.text: Not discussed in the FGD; no participant addressed how long a building plan approval/permit remains valid before lapsing or requiring renewal.

fees.text: Application fee ₹700 (non-refundable); building fee ₹80/sqm (residential) or ₹270/sqm (commercial); scrutiny fee ₹18/sqm (both uses), giving a combined ₹98/sqm residential and ₹288/sqm commercial; change-of-land-use fee cited in one case at roughly ₹33-34 lakh.

steps.title: Obtain change-of-land-use (CLU) certificate first, where required (commercial buildings or residential plots over 1 kanal)
Submit application online with revenue records (mutation), building plan and Aadhaar, within municipal limits (offline at the district beyond those limits)
Pay application fee, building fee and scrutiny fee on built-up area online
Drawing scrutinised via third-party Auto DCR software; objections raised and file reverted for rectification with no fixed resubmission deadline
Applicant separately pursues NOCs from multiple departments (electricity, water, fire, health, etc.)
Permission issued once NOCs are complete and fees paid; status trackable online, including which officer holds the file
Completion certificate and Occupancy Certificate sought post-construction, repeating roughly 70-80% of the same documents/steps, plus a further NOC after occupancy
steps.note: Described as a near-duplicate of the initial approval process.

remarks: FGD-only record (Mode B); the service maps to what the FGD titled 'Building Plan Approval', which flows through both the Housing Department's own online portal and the JK Single Window / National Single Window System.
A departmental representative acknowledged revenue records are not yet fully digitised, which can cause an auto-generated plot number to not match actual ground records.

gaps.text: No participant or department representative gave a single authoritative timeline figure; the stated '30 days approval / 21 days NOC' periods and a cited real-world ~3-month case were not reconciled.
The precise full list and count of NOCs required, beyond electricity, water supply, fire and health named individually, was not captured.

Deemed approval was described as existing 'subject to conditions' but participants indicated that in practice the applicant must simply wait for the officer to act, leaving its actual operability unclear.

Online submission, status tracking (including which officer holds the file) and NOC document carry-forward within the portal were described as working well, and a recent reform fixing department-wise NOC-issuance timelines was welcomed.
Participants' clearest asks were consolidating NOCs to title verification (plus safety NOCs like fire) for routine cases, and merging the change-of-land-use fee with the building fee.
The validity period of a granted building plan approval/permit (how long before it lapses or needs renewal) was not discussed.

findings.text: The service has no online route at all; the application form must be obtained physically from the department, and about 70% of UT departmental services were said to remain offline.
The application physically travels across about eighteen tables before sanction, and the applicant must follow it at each stage.

Sanction is valid 3 months before physical connection (extendable by a further 3 months), but charges begin from the end of the first 3 months regardless of whether the unit has actually been energised.
Surrendering a connection is considerably more cumbersome than obtaining one, requiring a no-dues certificate spanning other departments and reportedly taking up to a year.
A transformer costing ₹3-4 lakh must be installed and borne by the applicant, a significant cost for units whose total investment may be only ₹20-30 lakh.
Power-cut schedules are not published; interruptions of 8-12 hours occur with no advance intimation, unlike other states that notify planned cuts.
No prescribed or published timeline exists for a connection; one industrial case took about a year and a half following an initial rejection, while commercial connections took about ten days.
The security deposit is high, held idle with the bank and unavailable to the unit holder, and discourages applicants from declaring their full load.
Each department (including electricity) requires clearances issued by other departments rather than enforcing only its own mandate.
Remarks of 'no feasibility' are sometimes recorded on file without verification, even where load is actually available on the line.
A notarised affidavit before a first-class magistrate was identified as the principal unnecessary requirement, duplicating Aadhaar, proof of residence and land record already furnished.
A first application was rejected without substantive reasons, with the second application then taking several further months.
Bring the service online with digital forms, applications and status tracking.
Accept self-attestation instead of a magistrate affidavit, consistent with the broader self-certification policy.

Since smart-meter installation, no inspection is carried out and billing is reported as accurate and timely; power availability is no longer described as a constraint for industry, with the difficulty now lying in process rather than supply.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Power Development Department / electricity distribution division (application form obtained in person; file moves physically across field, division and sanctioning tables within the department).

portal.name: No online portal currently available for this service — entirely offline/physical process

timeline.basis: No official timeline is prescribed or published; participants reported commercial connections taking about 10 days and one industrial connection taking about a year and a half (roughly 547 days) following an initial rejection.
timeline.text: Timelines vary widely by connection type and were never officially communicated to applicants in advance.

documents: Application form (obtained physically from the department)
Notarised affidavit before a first-class magistrate
licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED. Beyond the magistrate's affidavit, Aadhaar, proof of residence and land record, no further document checklist was detailed.

deemedApproval.text: Participants stated they were not aware of any deemed-approval provision for electricity connection.

validity.text: Sanction for connection is valid for three months before physical/energised connection is required, with a further three-month extension available; charges are levied from the end of the first three months regardless of whether the connection has actually been energised.

fees.text: A connection fee of about ₹2,000 was cited for one participant's category, rising with sanctioned load; a security deposit (described as high) is also charged and held by the bank for the life of the connection without being available to the unit holder; a transformer costing about ₹3-4 lakh must additionally be installed and borne by the applicant in many cases.

steps.title: Obtain application form physically from the electricity department (no online download)
Submit the form with Aadhaar, proof of residence, land record and a magistrate-sworn affidavit
File is examined and physically routed across roughly eighteen tables/stages within the department
Electricity department alone inspects the premises/site; no joint inspection with other departments
Sanctioned-load-based connection fee and security deposit assessed and paid

Connection sanctioned; physical/energised connection due within an initial 3-month window (extendable by 3 more), with charges running from the end of the first window regardless of actual energisation

remarks: FGD-only record (Mode B); participants stated this service remains entirely offline, with no online application, tracking or status visibility, unlike most other JK services discussed in other FGDs.
Surrendering a connection was described as considerably more cumbersome than obtaining one, reportedly taking up to a year and requiring a no-dues certificate from other departments.

gaps.text: No official or published timeline exists for this service; actual durations reported by participants (10 days to ~1.5 years) could not be reconciled into a defined benchmark.
The exact connection-fee schedule by category/load and the security-deposit amount/formula were not captured beyond scattered participant examples.
Smart-meter rollout has removed the need for manual inspection and is reported to have made billing accurate and timely.

Participants' clearest asks were bringing the service online, replacing the magistrate affidavit with self-attestation, and aligning the pre-energisation charge-free window with actual construction timelines.

It is unclear whether 'no feasibility' recorded on a file reflects an actual technical constraint or an administrative default, since participants allege it sometimes does not reflect real line capacity.

findings.text: Compliances needed at the premises are not shown on the portal when applying; the officer's site visit is typically the first time the applicant learns what is pending, so the NOC is rarely granted at the first visit.
No official public helpdesk exists; applicants obtain an officer's personal phone number informally.
No refund provision exists for an accidental double payment.
Fire-safety norms such as two staircases are difficult to meet in old, narrow-laned buildings in old Jammu city, though occupant safety cannot be compromised.
Session FNO_1 participants said no defined processing timeline is known in advance, though no individual step was described as difficult.
Only a digitally signed scanned copy of the NOC is issued, not a physical original, which has occasionally caused difficulty during internal company audits.
Inspecting officers' own visit schedules add to coordination time; one applicant needed about three rounds of interaction before completion.
Validity is reported as two years (up from one) in one session, versus six months before renewal in the other session, with other departments (e.g., Pollution Control) granting three to five years.
Requirements are set by occupancy type (residential, hazardous, institutional), not by the pollution-category or room-count schemes used by other departments.
Application is made via the JK Single Window, which redirects to the department's own section; offline filing is not permitted per government guidelines.
Building plan approval and Aadhaar must be resubmitted at renewal even though already on file.
Where the department seeks a correction/clarification, the timeline extends with no prescribed outer limit.
The single window was unavailable for several months (reported as 8-10 months) in the previous year, attributed to a cyber attack.
Senior-officer review of the field officer's report/recommendation adds a further internal processing step before the NOC can be issued.
Display required compliances on the portal at application time so applicants can prepare before the officer's first visit.
Align Fire NOC validity with other departments (e.g., 5 years with annual inspection) instead of a 1-2 year cycle.

This year's FNO session-1 experience was described as smooth with the NOC received on time and no harassment, a marked contrast to earlier years; none of the FNO_1 participants needed a consultant, and the form was called the simplest among licences they had applied for online.

quotes.speaker: Industry User
quotes.quote: None of the compliance requirements — hydrants, extinguishers, sprinklers — were seen as unnecessary; these are directly related to protecting our people and property, not merely a departmental requirement.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Fire & Emergency Services Department, Jammu & Kashmir (local Fire Station / Fire Officer for inspection; application addressed to the Director of the department).

portal.name: JK Single Window (redirecting to the Fire Department's section); also reportedly available via the Jan Sugam application

timeline.basis: The department's internally cited turnaround is 30 days; session FNO reported NOCs typically received within about 20 days, while session FNO_1 reported approximately one to two months (up to ~60 days).
timeline.text: No written, publicly available timeline was identified by either session; reported actual durations range from about 15-20 days to 1-2 months.

documents: Firefighting-facility details (fire extinguishers, hydrant systems, etc., where applicable)
Aadhaar and GST certificate (not mandatory, attached where applicable)
licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED. Document lists given across the two sessions (building plan approval + application form in one session; firefighting-facility details, building plan and land deed in the other) broadly overlap but are not identical.

deemedApproval.text: Neither session described a deemed-approval mechanism for a fresh Fire NOC; the topic was discussed mainly in relation to renewal.

validity.text: Reports differ between sessions: one describes a first-time validity of two years (previously one year) for a departmental fee of ₹1,000; the other, held about seven weeks earlier, describes a six-month first-time validity before renewal is required, with participants there suggesting an extension to two-three years. This discrepancy is not resolved in the transcripts.

fees.text: A flat statutory charge of roughly ₹1,000 (cited as ₹1,000 for two years in one session, and as a flat ₹1,000 line-item with no further break-up in the other). Actual compliance cost (fire hydrant systems, pumps, piping, tanks, extinguishers, detectors) is considerably higher — cited at roughly ₹20-25 lakh for one manufacturing unit — and was regarded as a necessary safety investment rather than a regulatory burden.

steps.title: Create a profile on the JK Single Window (name, email, PAN, address, parentage, mobile, organisation type), select Fire NOC, and get redirected to the department's section
Upload documents (building plan approval, application form / firefighting-facility details, land deed) addressed to the Director; tracking ID generated
Application forwarded to the local Fire Station/Fire Officer; applicant contacted to fix a mutually convenient inspection date
Officer inspects premises against a checklist (extinguishers, CO2 cylinders, water tanks, smoke detectors, hydrant systems for larger premises)
Field officer's report/recommendation reviewed by a senior officer before the NOC is issued
NOC downloaded from the portal as a digitally signed, scanned/typed document (no physical original provided)

remarks: The two FNO sessions report different first-time validity periods (two years vs six months), not reconciled in either transcript — see the VAGUE gap below.
Session FNO_1 noted applicants receive only a digitally signed scanned copy, not a physical original, which occasionally creates difficulty during internal company audits.

gaps.text: The two FGD sessions report different first-time validity periods for a fresh Fire NOC — two years (up from one) in the 15-10-26 session versus six months in the 24-08-2026 session — not reconciled in either transcript; it may reflect a recent policy change between the two dates or inconsistent participant experience.

Neither session gives a complete, reconciled document checklist; one lists only 'building plan approval and the application form', the other lists 'firefighting facility details, the building plan and the land deed'.

Both sessions report the online application itself as comparatively simple and functional (one calling it 'the simplest' of all licence forms applied for), with documents already on the single-window profile (e.g., from the Pollution Control Committee) reusable for the Fire NOC application.

The clearest, twice-raised reform ask is extending first-time/renewal validity closer to the 3-5 year periods other departments grant, paired with annual inspection rather than frequent full reapplication.

No participant in either session identified the issuing authority's exact statutory processing deadline beyond an internally cited '30-day turnaround' (session FNO_1); whether this is a formally notified timeline or an internal departmental target was not clarified.

findings.text: The fee for petrol-pump nozzle calibration has risen roughly ninefold (from about ₹750/1 year to ₹6,000/2 years per nozzle); no rationale was given despite a grievance being raised.
Payments are sometimes debited but not received by the department, with the bank unable to trace them; there is no option on the portal to lodge a complaint about such failures.
A new 'project' must be created for every individual dispensing unit/nozzle, with the application repeated each time.

The circle/division is not auto-selected from the saved address at the time of payment, risking fees paid to the wrong circle; no refund or transfer is allowed in such cases, requiring a fresh application and payment.
The process is long and difficult for individual users (e.g., an auto driver), who mostly depend on third parties or common service centres.
A user manual and videos exist but do not clearly explain fields (e.g., land details), leaving individuals unable to complete the form unaided.

Fare-meter certificates remain handwritten and must be collected in person, while the dealer licence itself is computer-generated; contrasted unfavourably with Punjab's fully computer-generated certificate.
Upload size/format limits are difficult to meet from mobile photos, with no in-portal resize tool.
Verification dates for different machines at one premises drift apart once any one machine is recalibrated early, leaving a single premises with multiple renewal dates.
A dealer licence is valid for one year only, with no option to pay double for a two-year term.
Re-verification required within the already-paid validity period (e.g., after a seal is broken for repair) requires the full fee to be paid again, with no partial/component-based charge.
The single-window helpline is reported as unresponsive, and portal complaints receive no reply beyond being told 'it will be looked into'.

Documents stay on the portal but are tied to a specific project, so the same documents (including the licence itself) must be re-uploaded for every new project/service; roughly 80% of basic information (Aadhaar, PAN, establishment particulars) is re-entered at every renewal.
Land and workforce-size fields are asked even of individual applicants (e.g., an auto driver) who already hold a licence.

Calibrating a dispensing unit needs the oil company's own permission to break the seal, applied for in parallel on the company's own portal and the single window, coordinated by phone with the company's technician.

Limited inspector numbers, assigned area-wise, delay work if the inspector is engaged elsewhere that day; the technician and inspector must both be present the same day, and if either is unavailable the visit is deferred.
Allow one project per pump covering all dispensing units, rather than a new project per unit.

Late fees are calculated automatically and shown on the portal, with officers not insisting on them for a day or two's delay; query notifications by SMS/email worked satisfactorily in session LEM_1, and no officer was said to have demanded money in this service.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Legal Metrology Department, Jammu & Kashmir (Controller / Assistant Controller / Deputy Controller / Inspector hierarchy).

portal.name: JK Single Window portal (Legal Metrology service module; confirmed not on the National Single Window System)

timeline.basis: Session LEM participants cited 10-15 days for weighing-scale traders/manufacturers and 30 days for pumps/fare meters; session LEM_1 described only an informal, undocumented departmental instruction to apply a month before expiry, with no written timeline.
timeline.text: No officially published timeline exists; internally cited windows range from 10-15 days to 30 days depending on instrument type.

documents: Electricity bill (owned premises) or rent agreement (rented premises)
licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED.

deemedApproval.text: Participants in both sessions stated no auto/deemed-approval provision exists for Legal Metrology services.

validity.text: Instrument verification (e.g., petrol-pump nozzles) is valid for two years (previously one year); a dealer licence itself is valid for one year only, with no option to extend to two years by paying double.

fees.text: Petrol-pump nozzle calibration: ₹6,000/nozzle for 2 years (previously ₹750/nozzle for 1 year per session LEM_1), so a 4-nozzle pump pays ₹24,000. Tanker calibration fee risen from about ₹650 to about ₹1,300. Weighing-scale fee by class/capacity/premises type: e.g., ₹400 for a 30kg class-2 scale (session LEM); ₹200/unit at office premises or ₹400 at trade premises for class-2, rising to ₹300 (50kg) and ₹350 (100kg) (session LEM_1).

steps.title: Create an ID on the JK Single Window, complete the common application form, create a project, and select the Legal Metrology service (no provision to apply via the department's own website)
Upload documents (Aadhaar, PAN, site plan, model approval, manufacturer's licence/authorisation, electricity bill or rent agreement)
Pay the calculated fee (per nozzle/per scale, by class and capacity) online
For dispensing units, coordinate a joint visit date with the legal metrology inspector and the oil company's technician (needed to break the seal)
Inspector (sometimes with Assistant/Deputy Controller) verifies/calibrates the instrument on site (10-20 scales/day) or at the office (fare meters can be same-day)
Certificate/licence issued — computer-generated for a dealer licence, handwritten for a fare-meter certificate

remarks: The fee has risen sharply and recently (reported as roughly ninefold for petrol-pump nozzle calibration) without an explained rationale in either session; a grievance on this was said to remain unanswered.
Session LEM_1 explicitly states Legal Metrology is not yet on the National Single Window System, unlike several other JK services discussed elsewhere.

gaps.text: The two sessions give slightly different fee histories for nozzle calibration (session LEM: current ₹6,000/nozzle/2yrs described as 'about nine times' the earlier fee without a before-figure; session LEM_1: explicitly ₹750/1yr → ₹6,000/2yrs) — broadly consistent in direction and scale but not identical in the baseline figure cited.
Neither session gives the full fee schedule across all instrument types/classes; only scattered examples (nozzle, weighing scale by capacity/premises type, tanker calibration) were captured.

Query notifications by SMS/email were described as functioning well in session LEM_1, and the online application was described (session LEM) as otherwise usable once learned, with status trackable and officer numbers often displayed at pumps for direct help.

The clearest, most specific reform asks are a single project per pump (covering all dispensing units) and electronic generation of the fare-meter certificate, matching the computer-generated dealer licence and Punjab's practice.

It is unclear whether a formal grievance-redressal/ticketing mechanism exists for this service at all — session LEM participants said they were unaware one existed, while session LEM_1 participants described lodging complaints that went unanswered.

findings.text: No training, user manual or tutorial video exists for the renewal process; applicants rely on cyber cafes, whose operators use the unit's own login because the applicant does not know how to run the portal.
The form contains technical terms (e.g., types of fire-extinguisher cylinders) unfamiliar to a layperson.
A failed online payment with no offline option forced one applicant to obtain a bank demand draft and submit it manually.
No SMS is received at each processing stage; the applicant must log in to check status.
The departmental fee (₹1,000) is flat regardless of property size; participants want larger properties to pay more.
Relaxations (e.g., accepting windows instead of a second staircase) are given for old buildings in old Jammu city, while new properties must fully comply.

Some applicants received only a short provisional renewal (as little as one month) instead of the usual one-to-two-year term, due to a minor inspection deficiency, requiring early reapplication; the flat ₹1,000 fee is still charged on these short renewals.
Inspection duration varies widely — roughly 10 minutes for a small property to 3-4 hours for a large hotel — affecting overall processing time.
No defined per-level internal processing time exists, making it hard to pinpoint where a delayed case is stuck.
Documents (previous NOC, application form, approved building plan) are requested again at every renewal despite the single-window portal nominally maintaining a document repository.
The single window was unavailable for roughly 8-9 months in the previous year (session RFNO).
Incomplete documents leave remarks recorded and the application waiting until the applicant responds, with no fixed turnaround.
Grant a longer renewal validity (e.g., 5 years), since installations are already in place, keeping only the first NOC provisional for one year.
Fix a binding per-level processing-time window with accountability/penalties for officers who exceed it, mirroring the penalties applicants face for late renewal.
Implement the deemed-approval provision transparently, including clarity on fee payment under a deemed-approval scenario, and publish data on how often it is actually granted.

Session RFNO_1 participants described the renewal process as considerably smoother/faster than a few years ago and as one of the better-functioning government services; most completed it without a consultant, inspection visits are intimated in advance, and queries were site-specific rather than generic.

quotes.speaker: Industry Users
quotes.quote: There is no deemed approval, and without an inspection it would not be right either, as the compliances may not be in place.

quotes.speaker: Industry User

quotes.speaker: Industry User

quotes.speaker: Industry User
quotes.quote: Even though our documents are already saved in our single-window account, we still have to scan and upload them again for every renewal.

quotes.speaker: Industry User
quotes.quote: Deemed approval is provided for in the guidelines, but in practice it is not implemented for this service.

licenses.issuingAuthority: Fire & Emergency Services Department, Jammu & Kashmir (same department as fresh Fire NOC).

portal.name: JK Single Window (and possibly the Jan Sugam application, per one unverified participant claim)

timeline.basis: A government order reportedly sets 21 days for renewal; session RFNO participants reported one case taking 28 days, while session RFNO_1 participants reported most renewals completed in 15-20 days to one month, with a smaller number taking two to three months.
timeline.text: A stated 21-day order exists, but actual experience spans roughly 15 days to up to 3 months across the two sessions.

licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED.

deemedApproval.text: Session RFNO participants said no deemed-approval provision exists for renewal (and that deemed approval without inspection would be inappropriate given safety compliances); session RFNO_1 participants said a deemed-approval provision exists in departmental guidelines but is not implemented in practice. The two accounts are not reconciled in either transcript.

validity.text: Session RFNO describes a uniform two-year validity (up from one), introduced that year, versus three/five/eight/ten years in other states. Session RFNO_1 describes discretionary, inconsistent outcomes ranging from one month (provisional) to six months, one year, or two years depending on inspection findings and departmental discretion.

fees.text: A flat statutory fee of ₹1,000, payable on every renewal application regardless of property size or whether the renewal granted is a short provisional term.

steps.title: Log into the JK Single Window (or possibly Jan Sugam app, unverified), select Renewal of Fire NOC, upload documents and submit
Provide a self-declaration/affidavit (via an executive magistrate, available in 1-2 days; or, per a newer order cited by one participant, a simple undertaking)
Pay the flat ₹1,000 fee online
Officer inspects the premises against the prior online declaration/checklist, checking cylinder expiry/certification and any plan changes
steps.note: Deficiencies can trigger a short-term/provisional renewal (as little as one month) rather than the standard 1-2 year term, requiring early reapplication.

steps.title: Renewed NOC issued, nominally within 21 days per a government order, though actual duration ranges from about 15 days to up to 3 months

remarks: The two sessions give different accounts of deemed approval: one says no such provision exists at all; the other says a deemed-approval provision exists in departmental guidelines but is not implemented in practice — not reconciled in either transcript.
Relaxations (e.g., accepting windows in place of a second staircase) are reportedly given for old buildings in old Jammu city, while new properties must comply fully.

gaps.text: The two sessions disagree on whether a deemed-approval provision exists at all — session RFNO participants say no such provision exists; session RFNO_1 participants say it exists in departmental guidelines but is never implemented in practice. Neither transcript reconciles this.

Reported renewal validity varies widely and inconsistently — session RFNO cites a uniform 'two years, up from one' figure, while session RFNO_1 describes discretionary outcomes ranging from one month (provisional) to six months, one year or two years depending on inspection findings.

Session RFNO_1 participants described marked improvement over recent years, inspection visits intimated in advance, and queries limited to genuine site-specific deficiencies rather than generic objections.

The clearest, concrete reform ask is a binding per-level processing-time window with officer-side accountability (mirroring applicant-side late-renewal penalties), paired with transparent implementation of deemed approval.
Neither session specifies the exact criteria that trigger a short provisional renewal versus a full-term renewal, beyond 'a minor deficiency' being cited.

findings.text: No timeline is prescribed or communicated for refund processing; outcomes ranged from two months to eight-nine months to over a year, described by participants as depending on 'the mood of the department'.
Invoices that validate correctly on the taxpayer's own system fail validation at the department's end for reasons neither side can explain, with the refund withheld meanwhile.
An inverted duty structure (18% input tax vs 5% output tax in pharmaceuticals/plastics) leaves input tax credit structurally blocked, a direct cost to the business.
No grievance raised by any participant had ever been resolved; reminders go unanswered, and officers themselves attribute the problem to 'the portal'.
Applicants must physically visit the tax office roughly once or twice a month while a refund is pending, since the process otherwise does not move.
Notices are sometimes issued years after the relevant period (one example: an FY2022-23 notice issued in 2026), by which point records are hard to reconstruct.
No interest is paid on a refund delayed beyond a year, while even a single day's delay by the taxpayer attracts a compounding penalty.
Where a supplier defaults or closes down after a transaction, the purchaser's input tax credit is reversed and notice issued to the purchaser, despite the invoice and payment being on record.
No mechanism exists to carry forward an accidental tax overpayment against the following month (as existed under the earlier tax regime); it must instead be claimed back as a refund.
The refund is validated automatically against GSTR-2B and the monthly return, and proceeds only where invoices match.
No notification is issued where an error is found in the refund application; participants must find and correct it themselves.
Once an amount is deposited it cannot be edited, though pre-deposit corrections are possible.
Prescribe a definite refund timeline on the income-tax model (one to two weeks, with a stated expected date).
Release the refund and scrutinise afterward (issuing a notice only if a demand later arises), so working capital is not blocked pending verification.
Correct the inverted duty structure by aligning raw-material and finished-goods GST rates in pharmaceuticals/plastics.
Make the portal grievance mechanism actually respond to and resolve complaints.

GST registration (seven to ten days, no premises visit, no fee) and monthly filing (same-day, drafts saved, details pre-fetched) were both described as working well, in clear contrast with the refund process specifically.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: There is no timeline for a refund. It depends on the mood of the department.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: The invoice is valid and validates on our portal, but when the department validates it, it does not.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Our input is eighteen per cent and the finished product is five per cent. That gap cannot be managed.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Not one grievance raised by any of us has ever been addressed.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: A notice for 2022-23 has been issued in 2026. Nobody remembers that far back.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: They do not pay interest on a delayed refund, but a single day late and there is a penalty on us.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: In income tax the refund comes within one or two weeks. The same system should be in GST.

quotes.speaker: Industry Representative
quotes.quote: Release the money and do the scrutiny alongside. If a demand arises, send a notice.

licenses.issuingAuthority: State Taxes Department, Government of Jammu & Kashmir — refund applications are processed by the assigned GST officer.

portal.name: GST portal (gst.gov.in), the centralised national portal

timeline.basis: No statutory timeline was communicated to participants; three cases were cited — about two months, eight to nine months, and more than a year — with no prescribed ceiling given by any source.
timeline.text: No prescribed refund timeline exists or was communicated; reported durations ranged from about two months in the fastest case to more than a year in the slowest.

documents: Invoices and related supporting documents, uploaded in the prescribed format on the GST portal (same account used for registration/filing)
licenses.documentsNote: FGD-only record, not yet verified against an official ED. Participants explicitly stated no document was seen as unnecessary for the refund process itself; basic particulars are fetched automatically at subsequent filings.

deemedApproval.text: No deemed-approval or automatic-refund mechanism was described for GST refunds specifically; participants explicitly contrasted this with income tax refunds, said to arrive within one to two weeks with a stated date.

validity.text: Not applicable in the usual sense; a GST refund is a one-time transactional claim rather than a licence with a validity period.

fees.text: No government fee is payable for filing a GST refund application (or for registration or monthly filing); the only cost cited is the chartered accountant's annual fee (around ₹70,000) for those who do not file themselves.

steps.title: File refund application on the GST portal using the same account as for registration/filing
Upload invoices and supporting documents, individually or in bulk, in the prescribed format
System validates invoices against GSTR-2B and the monthly return; refund proceeds only where invoices match
steps.note: Invoices that validate on the taxpayer's own system sometimes fail validation on the department's side for reasons neither side can explain.

steps.title: Department-side processing/decision, with no SMS/portal notification of application-stage errors; applicant must identify and correct errors themselves
Refund credited once validated and cleared; in practice requires repeated applicant visits (roughly once or twice a month) to move the file forward, since no prescribed timeline governs the officer
steps.note: Duration reported from about two months to over a year.

remarks: FGD-only record (Mode B); this session also discussed GST Registration and GST Tax Filing favourably as context, but the structured record here is scoped to the Tax Refund service (TRG) per the canonical service codes.

An inverted duty structure (18% input tax vs 5% output tax in pharmaceuticals/plastics) was reported as a major structural driver of blocked input tax credit and refund volume, separate from procedural delay.

Where a supplier has defaulted/closed after a transaction, participants reported the purchaser's input tax credit being reversed and a notice issued to the purchaser, despite the invoice and payment being on record.

gaps.text: No participant or official source gave a formal statutory timeline for GST refund processing (unlike income tax, cited by participants as 1-2 weeks); the actual range reported (2 months to over a year) could not be tied to any defined rule.
The specific technical cause of invoices validating on the taxpayer's system but failing at the department's end was not identified by participants or the officer present.

GST registration and monthly filing were both described as working well (fast, fee-free, no premises visit, auto-fetched details at next filing) — in clear contrast to the refund process, suggesting the problem is specific to refunds rather than GST administration generally.

The clearest, most concrete reform ask is 'release first, scrutinise alongside' — release the refund and verify afterward, issuing a notice only if a demand later arises, rather than withholding refunds pending full verification.

It is unclear whether 'funds availability with the department' (cited once as a reason refunds are held) is an acknowledged administrative practice or an informal participant perception; this was not substantiated further in the discussion.
